title: Đóng backdoor `toolRenderers` — `Object.freeze` + `Readonly` ở tầng kiểu
wave: 2 (M2 wave 2 — 'Làm cho disable trung thực': WI-1 nửa timer, WI-2, WI-4. Ba work item độc lập, không mục nào chặn mục nào. XS–S, ~3 ngày cho cả wave, WI-4 là XS.)
one_line: Make the built-in tool-renderer registry read-only so no plugin can silently repaint every tool's transcript for the whole process — while keeping the one supported way to supply a renderer (a tool definition that carries its own render function) working exactly as before.
user_visible_effect: None for core oh-my-pi: every built-in renderer renders byte-identically, because a fully-populated object literal that nobody mutates behaves identically once frozen, and all 14 in-repo consumers are reads. The visible change lands only on the out-of-repo plugins that were writing to the global — exactly the population the freeze exists to evict: their override stops taking effect, and because extension modules are strict-mode ESM the assignment now throws a TypeError at load time instead of silently succeeding. That is a loud failure replacing a silent one, which is the point. The sanctioned replacement (a tool definition carrying its own render call/result function) is untouched and still wins over the built-in for any tool that supplies one.

steps.instruction: Re-confirm zero writers before touching anything — this is the one precondition the whole item rests on, and it must be re-run on the day you implement, not trusted from this document. Run: `git grep -nE 'toolRenderers\[[^]]*\] *=|toolRenderers\.[A-Za-z_$]+ *=|delete toolRenderers' -- packages`. It must return ZERO hits. Then run the inventory: `git grep -n toolRenderers -- packages` and confirm you get exactly 14 hits across 5 files — `packages/tui/src/tools/index.ts:35,73`; `packages/tui/src/chat/tool-execution.ts:17,355`; `packages/coding-agent/src/cli/gallery-cli.ts:16,141,307,344`; `packages/coding-agent/test/gallery-cli.test.ts:18,79`; `packages/coding-agent/test/tools/apply-patch-renderer.test.ts:8,29,77,90`. If the count moved, stop and re-audit: a new writer means the freeze is no longer XS.

Apply the declaration change. Replace `export const toolRenderers: Record<string, ToolRenderer> = {` with `export const toolRenderers: Readonly<Record<string, ToolRenderer>> = Object.freeze<Record<string, ToolRenderer>>({`. The explicit type argument on `Object.freeze` matters: it types the object literal as `Record<string, ToolRenderer>` (so the 30 heterogeneous per-tool renderer types are checked the same way they are today) while the const's declared type carries `Readonly`, which is what makes a write a compile error. Leave all 30 entries and the two alias comments untouched.

Close the call instead of the literal: change the `};` on line 70 to `});`. Do not move the `setXdevRendererLookup(...)` line — it is a read-only closure and must keep working; it is in fact a useful thing for the test to lean on.

Write the freeze test. Import `toolRenderers` from the local source path `../src/tools/index` (not the package specifier — keep the test self-contained inside the package). Test 1 asserts the observable contract: an outside importer attempting `registry.probe_backdoor = someRenderer` is rejected. Because the test file is strict-mode ESM, that assignment throws a `TypeError`; assert the rejection, and do NOT assert that `Object.freeze` was called or that some internal flag is set — those assert implementation, not the contract. Note there is no cleanup to write: the object cannot be mutated, which is exactly why this test is full-suite safe (no shared-state restore needed, unlike the existing pattern in this repo where a writable global would force an `afterEach`). Test 2 proves the freeze did not break the sanctioned path: build an `AgentTool`-shaped object carrying its own `renderResult` (and `renderCall`), hand it to `ToolExecutionComponent` for a tool name that is ALSO a built-in key such as `bash`, drive it with `updateResult`, and assert the extension's own rendered bytes appear in `component.render(width)` after stripping ANSI. The name collision is deliberate and load-bearing: it is the only way to prove a custom renderer can still win over the frozen global rather than being shadowed by it.

Write the sanctioned-path test at the adapter layer. This is the distinct failure mode the freeze could introduce: a freeze that accidentally breaks the legitimate write path is what would push extension authors back toward mutating the global, so it deserves its own test at the layer where the definition becomes the tool the transcript renders. Construct a `RegisteredTool` whose definition carries a `renderResult`, pass it through `wrapRegisteredTools`, and assert the resulting tool's render output contains the extension's marker bytes. Do not assert on internals; assert on the rendered output. This test is currently blocked in this checkout — see the `gate` field for the unblock command.

Run the gates in the `verification` field in order. The first two are the ones that can actually run today; the `bun test` pair cannot, and that is a pre-existing environment condition, not something this work item caused. If the native addon has been built by the time you pick this up, run the test pair too — they are written to be the regression pin, not a proof the change works.

test_contract:
TWO contracts, one per test file, deliberately not redundant.

(1) `packages/tui/test/tool-renderers-frozen.test.ts` — 'A third-party importer cannot repaint core's built-in tool rendering for the process.' Observable failure if it regresses: a plugin that assigns `toolRenderers.grep = ...` silently takes over the transcript of every grep call in every session, for every other importer of the module, with no owner, no ordering, and no way to unload it. This is why the test is allowed to exist despite AGENTS.md's general hostility to tests of internal wiring: what is protected here is not private state but another consumer's output, which is the definition of an externally observable contract. It also does not assert that `Object.freeze` was called — asserting the mechanism rather than the guarantee is exactly the kind of test that survives a refactor but proves nothing.

(2) `packages/coding-agent/test/extension-tool-renderer-registration.test.ts` — 'The sanctioned path is unaffected by the freeze.' Observable failure if it regresses: a tool definition that carries its own `renderResult` renders its own bytes after the freeze. The failure mode this defends against is the subtle one — a freeze that breaks the legitimate write path does not crash anything loudly, it just pushes extension authors back toward mutating the global, undoing the entire point of the item while every test still passes. This test asserts rendered output, not that the adapter copied two fields.

The second test earns its keep by being at a different layer, not by restating the first: the first proves the global is closed, the second proves the door next to it is open. If you can only run one of the two in this checkout, run the first — it is the closer package to the change.

gate:
DONE when, in order:

  (a) `bun run --cwd packages/tui check:types` is green AND `bun run --cwd packages/coding-agent check:types` is green with the freeze applied. This is the only gate in this environment that can fail, and it is not a weak gate: it is the one that proves the `Readonly` annotation is what turns a future `toolRenderers.x = y` into a compile error rather than a runtime surprise.

  (b) `git grep -nE 'toolRenderers\[[^]]*\] *=|toolRenderers\.[A-Za-z_$]+ *=' -- packages` still returns zero hits — i.e. the change introduced no writer.

  (c) Both new test files exist and are committed even though they cannot execute here. They are the regression pin for whoever builds the addon next; deleting them because they are red is the failure mode this item is most likely to fall into.

  (d) NOT a gate: whether `bun test` passes. It cannot, in this checkout, for reasons that predate this work item. If the engineer reports 'tests are red', check whether the red is the missing native addon before investigating their change.

  On `gate_can_fail`: yes, and it was demonstrated rather than assumed. With the `Readonly` annotation applied, injecting a single line `toolRenderers.probe_backdoor = toolRenderers.bash;` into `packages/tui/src/chat/tool-execution.ts:355` makes `bun run --cwd packages/tui check:types` exit 1 with `src/chat/tool-execution.ts(355,3): error TS2542: Index signature in type 'Readonly<Record<string, ToolRenderer<unknown, unknown>>>' only permits reading.` That probe was run, captured, and the tree was reverted (`git status` clean apart from the untracked spec output). Without the `Readonly` annotation this gate would be structurally incapable of failing — `Object.freeze` on its own leaves the declared type writable, so the check passes and the backdoor reopens silently. That is the whole reason step 2 asks for both halves.
blocks: WI-7 (registerMode — M2 wave 5). The plan's explicit ordering: land WI-4 first so the unload work has a complete inventory of what must be released. A frozen global has nothing to release, which is what makes WI-7's resource audit tractable.
effort: XS — and smaller than the plan's own XS, because the change itself is two lines in one file. The bulk of the time is the two test files, and both are blocked on an environment condition rather than on design. Verified end to end in this session: the two-line change compiles clean in both consuming packages, passes lint and format, and the write-rejection was demonstrated failing as intended.
risk: The single most likely way to get this wrong is treating 'the tests are red' as 'my change is broken' and either deleting the tests or reverting the freeze to make them runnable. Both are wrong and both silently undo the item. The red is a pre-existing missing native addon; the change is provably safe without it. The second most likely mistake is bundling the optional export-map narrowing (`"./*"` at packages/tui/package.json:94) into this diff because it is described as adjacent — it changes the public surface, it is an unanswered open question, and it is not needed for the freeze. The third is freezing without the `Readonly` type: that version is a runtime-only guard, `bun check` still cannot catch a future writer, and the item's stated purpose (close the backdoor so it cannot silently reopen) is only half delivered.
open_questions: Should the `Readonly<>` type annotation land in WI-4 or wait for the 'WI-4b' the plan keeps deferring it to? The plan's own later sections (around its lines 7866 and 8076) admit that `Object.freeze` alone carries no enforcement mechanism and that the constraint must come from the type — but WI-4b appears nowhere in the M2 wave table, so today nothing owns it. Evidence gathered here says the type half is free: `Readonly<Record<string, ToolRenderer>>` type-checks clean against all 14 consumers in both packages, and it turns a write into TS2542. RECOMMENDATION: land it here, inside WI-4, and close WI-4b as 'already done'. This is a decision, not a blocker — if the reviewer disagrees, dropping it is a one-token revert and the freeze still stands on its own.

Who builds the native addon, and when? Both test files for this item — and a large fraction of the repo's test suite — are blocked on `packages/natives/native/pi_natives.darwin-arm64.node`, and bazel is not installed in this environment, so the documented build command cannot run here. This is not specific to WI-4, but WI-4 is the first M2 work item to hit it, and its stated verification command is therefore unrunnable. A M2-wide decision on 'tests that require the addon' versus 'tests that do not' would unblock several waves at once.

Is the value import of `@oh-my-pi/pi-natives` at `packages/tui/src/theme/theme.ts:3` worth splitting so that theme-dependent tests can run without the addon? That single import is what makes the entire tool-renderer registry unloadable in this environment — every renderer takes a `Theme`, so every renderer module transitively loads the addon. Out of scope for WI-4 and probably not worth it on its own merits, but it is the root cause and it is cheap to name now.

The item's goal — close the backdoor so it cannot silently reopen — is therefore only half delivered by the freeze alone. Add the `Readonly` type annotation. Keep the runtime freeze too — the type cannot stop a cast.
